Eleven pregnant garter snakes went to a San Francisco zoo, and now 62 of their young are in the wild

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.
  • Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).
  • They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.

In spring 2025, U.S. Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).

They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.

Sources indicate that after giving birth, the mothers were returned to the wild, the zoo says. The zoo’s team raised their young until they were significant enough to be released.

On November 10, 2026, the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens remarked 62 of those zoo-born garter snakes had been released this fall in San Mateo County.

It was the first release under a head-starting program for the endangered subspecies. The announcement does not say how many are still alive.

Industry observers note that the San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia) is a subspecies of the common garter snake. The zoo states it lives only in San Mateo County and a small corner of Santa Cruz County.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes red on the top of the head, a greenish-blue or blue belly, a wide pale stripe down the back and red and black stripes on the sides.

According to recent reports, A major loss of habitat came after World War II. In the 1940s, the sag ponds along Skyline Boulevard, small ponds in low spots along a fault line, held hundreds of the snakes.

By the 1960s, nearly all of those ponds had been drained and built over, according to the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy.

It has been revealed that the snake went onto the first federal endangered species list on March 11, 1967, six years before the Endangered Species Act of 1973. The zoo estimates that a couple thousand remain in the wild today.

Recent findings suggest that federal biologists blame illegal collection, construction, drought and saltwater in coastal ponds. Bullfrogs and largemouth bass are on the list too, because they eat the snakes and their prey.

That prey includes threatened California red-legged frogs, which the snakes rely on for food, the zoo indicates.

Industry observers note that since 2004, the conservancy and the National Park Service have restored and enhanced 33 acres (13 hectares) of wetland, grassland and coastal scrub for the snakes, according to Midpen’s 2025 release. The work added new ponds for breeding habitat.

It has been revealed that garter snakes give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. In this subspecies, birth comes in July or August. A litter can hold 6 to 35 babies, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile notes.

It has been revealed that after the 11 females arrived, the team scanned them with ultrasound. The early scans revealed that a goal of 80 to 120 live babies was feasible, Midpen reported in September 2025.

Later that month, the district estimated that the zoo’s Conservation Team was raising about 120 newborns.

The zoo had practice with the species. Its staff bred San Francisco garter snakes in the 1990s to work out how to keep them.

From 2005, they developed care protocols with the San Diego Zoo on housing, diet, growth tracking and parasite checks, Midpen stated in 2025.

Rochelle Stiles, the zoo’s director of field conservation, described the goal of the zoo’s snake rearing work.

“By providing these young snakes with a safe environment during their most vulnerable stage of life, we’re giving them a stronger start in the wild,” she stated.

In a recent development, head-starting works that way. The young are fed and sheltered until they are big enough to handle predators and competition for food, a method that also saved an endangered wallaby population in Australia.

In a recent development, each snake born at the zoo had a genetic test before it left, and the results set its destination. About one-third went back to the area where its mother had been caught.

According to recent reports, the rest went to several other populations that were short on both snakes and genetic variety. Isolated groups slowly lose diversity, the same problem behind a proposed genetic rescue for Lassen red foxes in northern California.

Disease data mattered too. Laura Patterson coordinates amphibian and reptile conservation statewide for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).

She said a CDFW survey for snake fungal disease, an emerging disease found in many wild snakes, “aided in the selection process.”.

The partners will not name the release sites. The zoo noted secrecy protects the snakes from collectors, cars and disease.

Recent findings suggest that midpen biologist Karine Tokatlian also commented on the release. “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” she stated.

Removal from the endangered list requires at least 10 viable, self-sustaining breeding populations. Each one needs at least 200 snakes.

U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) ecologists had already tested the idea on a computer. In a 2023 paper in PLOS ONE, a team led by Jonathan Rose of the USGS Western Ecological Research Center simulated newly introduced populations started with newborns, juveniles, adults or a mix.

Head-started juveniles gave those populations the best chance of lasting. Releases would have to continue for at least 15 years to keep the risk of near-extinction low, the model said.

Raising juveniles also takes fewer adults away from the donor site. Justin Sloan, acting deputy field supervisor at the USFWS Sacramento office, credited research, genetic testing, habitat work and specialized care.

Ariel Starr, a Midpen wildlife ecologist, looked beyond this one subspecies.

“The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species,” she stated.

According to recent reports, the November announcement gives no survival rate for the 62. It also does not say how long they had been out when it was posted.

Survival is low even for snakes born in the wild. One study found only 2 percent of females born live to age 5, according to the USFWS.

There is also a gap between the 2025 estimate of about 120 newborns and the 62 released. The zoo did not explain it.

It has been revealed that the 2023 model focused on snake demography. Its authors wrote that the genetics of the donor, captive and released snakes would also be a major concern for any reintroduction plan.

It has been revealed that more than 130 garter snakes were born at the zoo in 2026. They are being raised for a second round of releases in 2027. Monitoring of both rounds will show whether the populations at the sites grow.

In a recent development, rachel Townsend, a National Park Service wildlife biologist, put the first round in proportion. “Releasing these snakes is a significant moment, but it is one step of many in a much larger recovery effort,” she said.

In a recent development, the mothers are back in the wild. This fall, 62 of their young were let go at sites the partners will not name.

The information was obtained from the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens.

Cracks in public health grew in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In a recent development, it’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines.
  • In a recent development, but when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

In a recent development, it’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” claims Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”.

In a recent development, but when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin states. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

According to recent reports, domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” claims Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

Such problems do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”.

On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

According to recent reports, about a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in Newly introduced York and Wisconsin.

Sources indicate that as of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

It has been revealed that the United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that in the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

In a recent development, during the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

It has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy claims. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

Even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, notes Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and Upcoming York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

In June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks showed,” Handy says.

Sources indicate that but it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

It can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials revealed a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

The FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, stated Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”.

According to recent reports, sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she mentioned they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”.

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the Fresh York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

Recent findings suggest that without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, says Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”.

Starting in 2027, FDA prepares to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Industry observers note that outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, says Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to quickly contain outbreaks.

Industry observers note that “We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”.

When the WHO announced in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, notes the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Industry observers note that confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered.

Sources indicate that as cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

In a recent development, before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

It has been revealed that kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

By September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of new Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli indicates.

Sources indicate that information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli states. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the latest trial after early evidence in animals and people demonstrated the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

In a recent development, conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of new cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond quickly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli claims.

According to recent reports, the M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

According to recent reports, it’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

In a recent development, more than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

The United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” notes Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”.

Instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”.

The CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the New York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm says. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”.

In a recent development, the outbreak, which ended July 2, was quickly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm notes. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”.

The international collaboration had some successes, says virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

Recent findings suggest that hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

“The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a upcoming one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

Recent findings suggest that “We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become crucial,” Palacios claims. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”.

Grand Canyon hotels reopen 81 days after a deadly flood, echoing a 1966 disaster

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water.
  • For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.
  • On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water. In 1966, a flood wrecked 40% of the same pipeline project.

For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.

On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.

Industry observers note that they had been closed for 81 days. A flash flood on August 29 tore through Bright Angel Canyon, killed two hikers and badly damaged the pipeline that carries water to the South Rim.

According to recent reports, it was not the first time. In 1966, while that same pipeline was being built, a flood destroyed or carried off about 40% of the project, according to the National Park Service.

The park announced on November 18 that six South Rim lodges would reopen on November 20: El Tovar Hotel, Thunderbird Lodge, Kachina Lodge, Bright Angel Lodge and Maswik Lodge, along with Yavapai Lodge, which is operated by Delaware North.

On the same day, the park moved from Stage 4 to Stage 3 water conservation measures, which it called an important milestone in the restoration of South Rim water services.

Food and drink services will resume gradually, and the park is asking visitors to check its website for dining hours.

Sources indicate that conserving water is still notable. Guests, visitors and residents are asked to take shorter showers, turn off faucets when they are not in use and avoid unnecessary water use.

The flash flood hit Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area at about 2:30 p.m. on August 29. By the next morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail.

Nearly all of the footbridges over Bright Angel Creek were destroyed.

Metal structures and debris washed into the Colorado River, which was closed to river traffic. In steep terrain, heavy rain can trigger flash floods in mountain rivers faster than expected.

Two hikers from Granbury, Texas, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, died in the flood.

A member of their hiking group was reported missing, and the park noted in its September 8 update that one person remained unaccounted for.

The flood badly damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a 12½-mile pipeline built in the 1960s.

It carries water from Roaring Springs, on the North Rim side, down through the canyon and up to the South Rim, where it supplies drinking water and fire protection for every facility, including more than 800 historic buildings.

The park’s drinking water comes from a single spring connected to more than 6 miles of caves.

About 40% of the old pipeline between the Phantom Ranch area and the North Rim was damaged, and the water intakes at Bright Angel Creek and Roaring Springs were hit hard.

On August 31, the park stopped all overnight stays at its hotels, including Phantom Ranch, and the South Rim began living on stored water.

It has been revealed that the park stayed open for day visits. When it unveiled the closure, it remarked South Rim food and drink services, the Grand Canyon Clinic and the post office would remain open, some with reduced hours, while campers could only dry camp.

On September 16, a second flash flood damaged a temporary water intake that crews were building at Bright Angel Creek.

No one was hurt, but crews had to work out what repairs were needed and how the damage would affect the timeline.

On September 19, the park noted it expected to start pumping water from the creek to a new treatment plant by November 16, and it was working on an agreement to haul about 200,000 gallons of water a day to keep its tanks from running low.

At the time, the South Rim was using about 137,000 gallons a day.

By November 18, the park said water services to the South Rim were being restored, which allowed the hotels to reopen two days later.

The pipeline itself was born out of a water problem. From 1901 to 1932, the Santa Fe railroad brought drinking water to the South Rim by train every day, and the trains came back as needed until the late 1960s.

In the summer of 1961, a water train of 20 cars carried about 204,000 gallons.

Construction of the Transcanyon Waterline began in January 1965, using 6-inch and 8-inch aluminum pipe. Most of the equipment was designed specifically for the project, and the rest of the work was done by hand.

A year later, the project was nearly finished when what the park calls a 1,000-year flood struck.

Fifteen inches of rain fell on the inner canyon, and the water carried away trees, boulders and sections of new pipe.

A survey after the flood found that about 40% of the project was destroyed or missing. The cost rose from $2 million to $5 million, and construction resumed in late 1967.

The flood’s high-water mark is still recorded on the walls of the Phantom Ranch Ranger Station.

The old line was built to last about 30 years and has been in service for more than 50. Since 2010, it has suffered over 85 major breaks.

A single repair often costs more than $25,000, and crews can reach the inner canyon only by trail or helicopter.

Breaks had closed the hotels before. In December 2025, after three significant breaks since late October, the park suspended overnight stays on December 6 and reopened the lodges on December 17.

In 2023, the park began a $208 million project to replace the pipeline and modernize the water system.

The newly introduced pipeline on the south side of the canyon was not damaged by either flood this year, and before August 29 the park was just over a month away from starting to use it.

Some inner canyon trails reopened in late October, including the South Kaibab Trail below the Tipoff and the River Trail.

But the Black Bridge, the Silver Bridge, Phantom Ranch and the entire North Kaibab Trail remained closed, and the park warned that water would stay off at Mile-and-a-Half and Three-Mile Resthouses and at Havasupai Gardens for the rest of the winter.

Hikers must carry all their water and a way to filter or treat it.

According to recent reports, el Tovar, a National Historic Landmark since 1987, was built from local limestone and Oregon pine for nearly $250,000. The hotel, which has 78 rooms, is once again taking guests.

The park claims water conservation remains important as operations resume, and that the patience of residents, visitors and businesses during the emergency helped it keep essential services running.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s releases on the reopening of South Rim lodging, the August 29 flash flood, the recovery plan, the projected water dates, the August 31 hotel closure, the two hikers who died, the second flash flood, the trail reopenings and the December 2025 hotel reopening, its pages on the Transcanyon Waterline and its history, and its page on El Tovar Hotel.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday.
  • According to recent reports, more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E.
  • Sources indicate that but Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

Sources indicate that but Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete strategy” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”.

Sanders stated during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a upcoming and bold direction.”.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders noted, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”.

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”.

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking noted he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”.

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but mentioned she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete strategy that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”.

It has been revealed that she urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she mentioned, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”.

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to latest members who have just come off the campaign trail.”.

Recent findings suggest that “What I’ve stated from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”.

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Recent findings suggest that schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he stated of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

Recent findings suggest that “That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she stated.

Sources indicate that gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she mentioned.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

In a recent development, sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., remarked he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to blueprint together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”.

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”.

“Yes,” he mentioned of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”.

“And we can do that with Chuck Schumer.”.

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

#77436. Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1294 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.
  • Recent findings suggest that meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group.
  • In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.

Recent findings suggest that meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group. How well can one find its way alone?

In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.

After release, 18 reached a familiar spot or found their group. Fourteen headed first to the burrow where the group had slept.

The team found no clear advantage for older or more experienced animals.

The researchers suggest that daily group travel may give meerkats enough experience to navigate alone.

Sources indicate that the study was led by Mathilde Martin of the University of Zurich. The team worked alongside the Kalahari Meerkat Project, which follows about 15 wild groups accustomed to people.

The project is run from the Kalahari Research Centre, which is known as the KRC.

“At the KRC, our work with meerkats allows us to distract them with a water bottle and fit their collar in a few seconds while they stand upright drinking; a mere formality for them,” Martin remarked.

A GPS tag on each collar logged the position of the animal once every second. A radio transmitter was also fitted, along with a small audio recorder for the meerkat’s calls.

Recent findings suggest that the team tested a total of 20 adults from five groups between January and March 2025. Fifteen of these animals were male, whereas only five of them were female.

Each meerkat was caught while its group was foraging and was released up to 0.9 miles (1.5 kilometers) away.

Such a distance is greater than the ground usually covered by a meerkat group in a whole day.

Recent findings suggest that the release sites were located inside the territory of each group. The team chose areas that the group had not visited for at least 30 days.

Sources indicate that homing experiments of this kind have previously been carried out on honeybees and desert ants. Highly social animals that travel in tight groups have rarely been tested in the same way.

This is because the knowledge of one animal is difficult to separate from the decisions of the group.

Eighteen of the 20 meerkats left the release site. The sleeping burrow, the capture spot or the group itself was reached by all 18 of them.

Some of the meerkats departed almost at once, whereas others circled the release site for nearly 90 minutes.

The area covered by them ranged from half an acre to almost 17 acres (2,050 to 68,200 square meters).

A meerkat rarely strayed from its course once a direction had been chosen. Sixteen of the animals aimed for a fixed place.

The sleeping burrow was visited first by 14 of those 16.

On average, the straight-line distance to the target amounted to 82% of the distance actually walked by the meerkat.

Recent findings suggest that the release areas had not been visited by the group for a month. The team therefore concluded that the meerkats had been navigating from long-term memory.

According to recent reports, two males never left the release site, and they were carried back to their groups after 90 minutes. They were no younger or less experienced than the others.

The authors suspect that stress kept them there, and not a lack of knowledge.

In a recent development, some meerkats had been expected to navigate better than others. Subordinate males sometimes leave the group and go alone in search of mates.

Other females are occasionally driven out for a while by the dominant female.

According to recent reports, solo trips of this kind could be counted as practice. The researchers also considered the age of each animal, together with the time it spent on guard duty.

Attention was given as well to how often it scent-marked the territory or dug at shelters.

None of those traits predicted how long a meerkat explored. Neither did they predict how accurately it set off or how straight it travelled.

No clear difference was found between males and females either, although only five females took part.

Industry observers note that the authors think that the explanation lies in the territory itself. It is small and stable, with 0.3 to 0.6 miles (0.5 to 1 kilometer) covered by a group daily.

The whole territory has probably been crossed several times by each member by the time adulthood is reached.

The authors wrote that pigeons of different ages are likewise able to find their way home equally well.

Sources indicate that on the way home, the meerkats spent about two-thirds of their time searching for cues. Most of the remaining time was spent moving.

Few of them stopped to eat, and those that did only grabbed millipedes crawling on the sand.

Industry observers note that the animals stood upright or climbed a bush or tree trunk in order to scan the landscape. Overall, they spent 10 times longer on looking than on sniffing.

In a recent development, this balance between looking and sniffing was altered late in the trip. By that stage, a meerkat had reached its target and was searching for its group. Sniffing then took up more than 20% of its cue-searching time.

Along the way, meerkats were often seen sniffing around boltholes. These are the small shelters that the animals dig across their territory. An earlier experiment had found that meerkats remember where their boltholes are.

The authors suggested that boltholes may serve as landmarks in a meerkat’s memory of its territory.

The search was not ended by reaching the burrow, because the group could have moved on since the capture.

Thirteen of the 20 meerkats rejoined their groups on their own. The slowest took almost three hours.

It has been revealed that the burrow or the capture site was reached by five others. The group had nevertheless not been found by them when the three-hour limit ran out.

These animals were caught again and returned by the team.

Industry observers note that the researchers could not explain why some meerkats succeeded while others did not. Success was not predicted by a straighter trip to the burrow.

Nor was it predicted by the number of scent marks left behind by the group.

Recent findings suggest that the tracking of a group was compared by the authors to a predator following its prey. The target keeps moving and its route is not known to the searcher.

In a recent development, twenty animals make up a small sample, as the authors wrote. All of them were subordinate adults older than 10 months, so pups and dominant animals were not tested.

Recent findings suggest that every release was also made inside familiar territory. The results therefore do not show how a meerkat would manage in a place it does not know.

Recent findings suggest that two reasons for looking around could not be fully separated either. A lone meerkat that scans the landscape may be checking for predators as much as searching for landmarks.

If many group members know the territory, the next question is who leads when the group moves.

The authors want to know whether certain traits influence which animal takes the lead. The physical needs of an animal and its social rank are two examples.

Co-author Benjamin Robira said the team now wants to understand what makes up a meerkat’s mental picture of its territory.

The researchers also intend to study how the animals get from one point to another.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter.
  • It has been revealed that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

It has been revealed that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

Sources indicate that first, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

It has been revealed that instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

It has been revealed that still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

It has been revealed that they’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

#77433. Industry News: Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (918 w)

Industry News: Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.
  • According to recent reports, some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs.
  • Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.

According to recent reports, some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs. Yet roughly half its living species arose within the past six million years, as mountains rose and landscapes changed.

Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.

In a recent development, the findings draw on decades of work identifying ferns and establishing where they grow. That groundwork made it possible to investigate how the group spread and diversified.

“We have conducted extensive research at the University of Turku in order to understand the biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest,” noted senior author Hanna Tuomisto, a professor of ecology.

“In the last 25 years, we have discovered and described 47 newly introduced Danaea species previously unknown to science, and have clarified the distribution and phylogenetic relationships of the species in the Danaea genus.”.

“We have now been able to link this information to the geological and climatic history of tropical America.”.

The team combined DNA evidence from 78 species with 2,289 verified records of where the ferns grow. These records helped reconstruct where ancestral ferns probably lived and the elevations they occupied.

The genetic analysis included 11 species that had not yet been formally described.

The researchers’ preferred estimate suggests that the Danaea lineage split from the lineage of its closest living relatives about 128 million years ago, during the Early Cretaceous.

Industry observers note that the common ancestor of its surviving species lived much later, around 53 million years ago. The researchers traced that ancestor to Amazonia.

But an ancient lineage need not consist of ancient species. About half of today’s Danaea species originated during the past six million years.

This complicates a familiar explanation for tropical richness: favorable conditions allowed species to accumulate over immense stretches of time.

Persistence mattered, but the landscape also kept changing, creating opportunities for newly introduced species.

Fern diversity generally reaches its greatest heights in tropical mountain forests. Danaea follows a different pattern: Amazonia has consistently held its largest pool of species in the reconstruction.

It has been revealed that “Mountain rainforests are home in particular to an abundance of epiphytes – plants that grow on top of other plants. Danaea ferns, on the other hand, grow on the forest floor,” noted lead author Venni Keskiniva, a postdoctoral researcher at Turku.

“These research results are, in fact, similar to those obtained for trees, which are also the most species-rich in lowland rainforests.”.

In a recent development, where a plant lives within a forest may therefore help explain where its group becomes most diverse. Findings from one fern group cannot automatically describe them all.

According to recent reports, the Andes still played an important role. Although Amazonia contained more species, the mountains became the leading source of dispersal to other regions.

Industry observers note that mountain formation affected far more than the slopes themselves. As the Andes rose, they changed rainfall patterns along with the soils developing across neighboring lowlands.

Recent findings suggest that vast wetlands once occupied much of western Amazonia. Their drainage near the end of the Miocene opened additional land for forest plants to colonize.

The resulting western Amazonian soils were generally richer in nutrients and more variable, than soils in central Amazonia.

Those differences may have encouraged plants to specialize in different environments.

In a recent development, the timing fits the fern history. Most newly introduced Amazonian species arising within the past six million years appeared in western Amazonia during the last three million.

According to recent reports, new land in southern Central America also offered room for expansion. Arriving lineages frequently gave rise to additional species as the region’s landscapes developed.

The first mountain-adapted Danaea lineages appeared around 20 million years ago, following an intensification of Andean uplift. Several later spread into regions farther from the equator.

Their earlier move uphill may have helped them cope with the conditions they encountered there.

“As the plants had already adapted to the cooler climate of the mountains, it may have been easier for them to spread to areas where the temperature differences between the seasons are greater,” Keskiniva noted.

Lineages that remained adapted to Amazonian lowlands tended to stay within that region.

The repeated sequence of mountain colonization followed by expansion suggests that climate tolerance influenced which routes were available.

According to recent reports, the mountains could both separate populations and help others reach newly introduced habitats. Their role changed as the landscape rose and different fern lineages established themselves.

Assigning dates to this history was difficult. Many relevant fossils are fragmentary, and researchers disagree about where they belong in the family tree.

The team compared three dating approaches, which produced substantially different ages. It favored the reconstruction most consistent with other biological and geological evidence.

Industry observers note that the dates remain estimates, and coinciding events do not establish a cause by themselves. Still, the findings connect the survival of ancient lineages with much younger episodes of diversification.

“The biodiversity in rainforests is the result of a long history, but its formation has also been greatly influenced by events that are relatively recent on a geological time scale,” Keskiniva concluded.

The study is published in the journal Frontiers of Biogeography.

Tech Report: Could a wasp the size of a sesame seed help protect carrots and canola?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists discovered Gonatopus quebecensis, a tiny wasp in Québec that attacks leafhoppers and might help protect crops naturally.
  • Some leafhoppers in Québec farm fields have a small sac stuck to their bodies.
  • Each sac holds a wasp larva that feeds on the leafhopper as it grows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists discovered Gonatopus quebecensis, a tiny wasp in Québec that attacks leafhoppers and might help protect crops naturally.

Some leafhoppers in Québec farm fields have a small sac stuck to their bodies. These insects are known to spread disease to carrots and canola.

Each sac holds a wasp larva that feeds on the leafhopper as it grows.

Sources indicate that the wasps were raised to adulthood by researchers, who found a species nobody had named. It has now been called Gonatopus quebecensis.

It belongs to a group known as pincer wasps and is about as long as a sesame seed.

Recent findings suggest that the wasp is a natural enemy of a crop pest and was already living in the fields. The researchers do not yet know whether it kills enough leafhoppers to help a farmer.

Leafhoppers on the province’s farms have been studied by scientists at Université Laval in Québec City since 2021.

Study supervisor Edel Pérez-López said the sightings “sparked our curiosity about the natural enemies of these important agricultural insects.”.

In a recent development, the study itself is a description. Lead author Thomas Vinatier and five colleagues described the wasp’s body and read a stretch of its DNA. The insect it grows on was also identified. The wasp was not tested as pest control.

Recent findings suggest that in July 2025 the team collected leafhoppers carrying wasp larvae. The insects came from highbush blueberry fields in the Mauricie region of Québec.

They were moved into a university greenhouse where the wasps bred on leafhoppers kept on potted barley. The room was held at 73°F (23°C) and the lights stayed on 18 hours a day.

Adult wasps emerged and the colony kept going. One female now serves as the reference specimen for the species. She was reared there in January 2026.

For close study the researchers randomly picked 11 adults. Six were females and five were males. Seven more were dissected so the mouthparts could be examined under a microscope.

Industry observers note that the reference female and one male are now stored in Ottawa. They are kept in the Canadian National Collection of Insects, Arachnids and Nematodes. The other specimens stayed at the university.

The newly introduced species is named after Québec. A total of 55 Gonatopus species are now known from the Nearctic region. That region covers most of North America.

According to recent reports, the female has no wings. She is mostly black with brownish-yellow on parts of her legs and antennae. At 0.12 inches (2.97 millimeters) long she could pass for a small ant.

Each of her front legs ends in a pincer. It is made of an enlarged claw and the last segment of the foot. A row of tiny plates is carried on that segment.

It has been revealed that pincers like hers give the family its common name. Females grab their prey with them. The family has 1,928 known species that attack leafhoppers and their relatives.

The male is a little smaller at just under a tenth of an inch (2.41 millimeters). He is almost entirely black and has clear wings.

In a recent development, males and females are hard to match in these parasitic wasps. The two sexes of one species can look very unlike each other. Matching them by eye is therefore unreliable.

Rearing helped because both sexes came out of the same colony on the same host. The match was supported by the DNA data.

In a recent development, A short stretch of a gene was read from four wasps. Two were females and two were males. Biologists use that stretch as a DNA barcode because it differs from one species to the next.

No named species in the public databases matched the four wasps. Two unnamed records did.

Recent findings suggest that one was a larva from Québec that the same lab had raised earlier from the same leafhopper species. It was a 99.91% match.

The other was an unidentified larva from Ontario. It was filed in a reference library of 1.5 million barcodes from Canadian invertebrates.

The Ontario larva’s barcode matched the females’ exactly and the males’ at 99.80%.

The wasp had therefore been collected and sequenced before in two provinces. It may have gone unnamed because no adult specimens were available.

Among the named species compared, Gonatopus pedestris had the most similar DNA barcode, at 95.74%.

Only one G. pedestris barcode was available for the comparison. It came from a specimen collected in Norway. The authors wrote that more samples are needed to show how the two species are related.

The wasp’s host is the aster leafhopper. This insect is about an eighth of an inch (3 to 4 millimeters) long.

The wasp’s larvae develop on the aster leafhopper and feed on it.

In a recent development, an infected aster leafhopper can pass along phytoplasmas as it feeds on a plant. Phytoplasmas are bacteria-like organisms that have no cell wall.

One result is aster yellows, a disease capable of heavy losses in canola and carrots.

The aster leafhopper is abundant on Canadian farms. In Québec strawberry fields it was found more often than any other leafhopper in the team’s earlier surveys.

In a recent development, spraying has not been a sure answer for these crop pests. Strawberry fields in eastern Canada were examined in a 2024 study by members of the same lab.

They reported that growers’ sprays may not have been keeping leafhopper numbers down.

In a recent development, the search for the leafhopper’s natural enemies had a second motive. Pérez-López mentioned it was the province’s push to use less insecticide.

In a recent development, the farming question was left open by the researchers. They do not yet know what share of leafhoppers the wasp attacks or at what time of year. It is also unclear whether other leafhopper species are used.

Sources indicate that wingless females are poorly sampled by the traps entomologists set for flying insects. Wasps like this one may therefore be undercounted across North America, the authors wrote.

It has been revealed that the team suggested repeating its own method in more places. Leafhoppers that carry wasp larvae would be collected and kept alive until the wasps emerge. The adults can then be matched by body and by DNA.

The authors wrote that such studies must come first. Only then can the wasp’s contribution to pest control be judged.

According to recent reports, three jobs are planned by Pérez-López’s lab. They are a full genome for the wasp, a closer look at its breeding and trials with other leafhopper species.

The full study was published in the journal ZooKeys.

#77429. Industry News: What could make a giant planet disappear? Astronomers may have the answer

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1149 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What could make a giant planet disappear? Astronomers may have the answer

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A giant planet stopped crossing its star as seen from Earth, and astronomers suspect an unseen neighbor tipped its orbit.
  • It has been revealed that astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years.
  • Recent findings suggest that the planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A giant planet stopped crossing its star as seen from Earth, and astronomers suspect an unseen neighbor tipped its orbit.

It has been revealed that astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years. Then, in March 2026, TESS looked again and saw no sign of a crossing.

Recent findings suggest that the planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere. Its orbit has tipped, most likely from the pull of a second planet in the same system, one that astronomers haven’t detected directly.

TOI-2535 b, more than 1,000 light-years away, is the first confirmed planet around a single star that astronomers have seen stop crossing.

Samuel Yee, a postdoctoral fellow at UCLA, led the study with astrophysicist Erik Petigura.

Each of those crossings is called a transit. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching,” Yee mentioned.

When a planet passes between its star and Earth, it blocks a little of the starlight.

The star dims for a few hours, and that small dip is how NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) finds fresh worlds.

A transit only shows up if the star, the planet and Earth line up almost perfectly.

If the orbit tips by just a few degrees, the planet passes above or below the star as seen from Earth, and the star never dims.

TESS checked on the star, called TOI-2535, five times between April 2019 and March 2026.

In a recent development, the planet orbiting it is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that orbits very close to its star. It goes around once every 8.24 days. Mercury takes 88 days, more than 10 times as long.

To confirm the planet, the team used an instrument on the 11.5-foot (3.5-meter) WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona.

The experts tracked how the star shifted back and forth, and the measurements ruled out a small star.

Industry observers note that most planets that cross their stars keep a steady schedule. TOI-2535 b’s crossings came as much as six hours early or late. No hot Jupiter that circles its star in under 10 days has a bigger timing swing on record.

Over the years, the crossings grew shorter and blocked less starlight.

A planet blocks less light, for less time, as its path moves from the middle of a star toward its edge.

Over seven years, the path likely moved across more than half of the star’s face. It passed the middle, grazed the edge, then missed the star entirely.

From the ground, the team tried 15 times and caught a crossing only six times, because the planet kept arriving when it wasn’t expected.

When TESS looked again in March 2026, it found no crossing anywhere in the window where the planet could have shown up.

Industry observers note that so what’s pulling on it? Planets in the same system tug on each other. If two orbits are tilted relative to one another, those tugs slowly swing the direction each orbit faces.

Recent findings suggest that the team’s computer models suggest the neighbor is at least as massive as Saturn, so it’s probably a second giant planet. The two likely move in a simple rhythm, such as one circling twice for every lap of the other.

By the models, the two orbits must be tilted at least 5 degrees apart to turn this fast.

In most tightly packed systems, orbits stay within 1 to 2 degrees of each other. If this tilt holds up, the system will be one of only a handful so far out of line.

Recent findings suggest that “We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits,” Yee remarked.

“We know of a few systems that are like this. This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly.”.

Petigura used Earth’s moon to explain it.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura mentioned.

It has been revealed that “But because the moon’s orbit is tilted, eclipses are less common. The tilt of the moon’s orbit is a relic of its violent formation history, which resulted from a collision with the early Earth.”.

The same geometry decides when TOI-2535 b will be back. The team calculated that each orbit goes through a full cycle every 30 to 50 years.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers expect the planet to start crossing its star again within that span. Its hidden neighbor could start crossing even sooner.

Early planet formation models suggested giant planets need lots of ice to form. So hot Jupiters probably formed far from their stars and moved closer later.

Industry observers note that how? Yee and Petigura see two ways. One is violent. A near-collision knocks the planet onto a stretched-out orbit, and the star pulls it in.

Industry observers note that the other is slow. The planet drifts inward with other planets through the gas and dust around a young star. This way should leave the orbits flat.

If the suspected giant neighbor is there, the two planets likely drifted inward together through the gas disk around their young star.

In a recent development, “Because TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,” Yee said. “We may be seeing a formation channel that doesn’t happen very often but is very interesting.”.

Recent findings suggest that the tilt is still a loose end. The researchers think parts of the system may have tugged on each other later, tipping the orbits over time.

Recent findings suggest that hundreds of hot Jupiters are known around other stars. Few have a planet close enough to change their orbits. When one does, the neighbor is almost always much smaller. The only other known exception is WASP-148.

The team can’t say how massive the neighbor is or where it orbits. The crossing times also scattered more than the models predicted.

According to recent reports, the star’s back-and-forth motion was jumpier than expected for an old, calm star, too. Both clues could mean there’s more than one unseen planet.

TESS’s first four years of data alone couldn’t have clearly shown the shrinking crossings.

According to recent reports, with no crossings left to time, the researchers wrote that the best way forward is to measure the star’s back-and-forth motion often. A neighbor as heavy as the models suggest should show up in that data on its own.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • House and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen.
