📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

House and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Industry observers note that republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Sources indicate that moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so notable,” the Ohio senator remarked in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his newly introduced role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”.

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

It has been revealed that moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is at the moment serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

In a recent development, brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored big wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In a recent development, in an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”.

Recent findings suggest that the 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

Recent findings suggest that on the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

Sources indicate that house Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Industry observers note that like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

Hawaii’s 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch was carved from lava that flowed about 550 years ago, and in late September it fell into the Pacific

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026.
  • For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.
  • Sources indicate that that view is gone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026. Here is how it formed and why sea arches eventually fall.

For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.

Sources indicate that that view is gone. The Hōlei Sea Arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, 2026. By the night of Sunday, September 27, it had collapsed into the ocean, the National Park Service announced on October 1.

The exact time of the collapse is unknown. According to the park, it could have happened while the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo.

The arch stood about 90 feet (27.4 meters) high and extended from steep sea cliffs into the ocean along the park’s southern coast, on the Island of Hawaiʻi.

According to recent reports, it was carved into the cliff of an ancient lava flow from about 550 years ago, according to the park. The arch took shape through what geologists call differential erosion: some layers of lava are harder than others, so the sea wears them away at different speeds.

Visitors could see it by walking a short distance from the end of Chain of Craters Road, which the park described in 2020 as a 19-mile drive through some of the most spectacular scenery in the park.

Recent findings suggest that the park’s own page on the arch was clear about one thing. The formation was beautiful but temporary, with a limited life span, and it would eventually crumble into the sea.

In a recent development, sea arches like Hōlei can be found along a wide stretch of Hawaiʻi’s southern coast. They are remnants of once-continuous sea cliffs, built where lava met the sea and added to the size of the island.

Lava meeting the sea can even build whole new land, as it did when a new island rose from the sea off Iceland in 1963.

Sources indicate that the moment that upcoming lava cooled and turned to rock, it began to erode, the park explains. The seas on the island’s southern edge are known for rough water and violent surf, and the waves slowly break apart the rock and carve sea caves into the cliffs.

When waves hit the back wall of a sea cave, the water bounces back and starts to erode the cave’s headland. Over time, that forms an arch.

The erosion does not stop there. Given enough time, the waves cause the remaining bridge of rock to collapse, leaving behind a pile of rocks known as a sea stack.

Volcanic coastlines are constantly being remade, and on the same island, Kīlauea has produced 55 lava fountains since December 2024.

The coastline around the arch had shown signs of instability for years.

In a recent development, earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs near the arch. In January 2020, new cracks and instability led the park to close the original viewing area and the short trail to it.

“This fresh development reminds us that Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is an ever-changing volcanic landscape,” Rhonda Loh, then the park’s acting superintendent, noted in January 2020.

A safer viewing area opened in March 2020, about 1,000 feet past the gate at the end of Chain of Craters Road and set back from the cliff edge.

Later that year, massive surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the lower part of the arch.

The park is urging visitors to stay back from the unstable cliffs, which drop vertically into the ocean and present a serious risk of falling.

After the collapse, photos on social media showed people entering the closed area near where the arch once stood.

According to the park, that puts both the visitors and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning off the rough, wave-swept coast.

Visitors are required to stay out of closed areas and away from cliff edges, which can collapse without warning.

The park describes individual sea arches as an ephemeral feature of the island’s constantly shifting coastline.

It has been revealed that as the cliff slowly migrates inland, other arches will form and replace Hōlei, the park states. The park notes that erosion does not stop once an arch has formed.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s announcement of the collapse, its pages on Hōlei Sea Arch and how sea arches form, and its 2020 releases on the closure of the overlook and the new viewing area.

#77424. A one-in-a-million catch in a New York harbor turns out to be a bright yellow burbot

A one-in-a-million catch in a New York harbor turns out to be a bright yellow burbot

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, Upcoming York.
  • Sources indicate that biologists with the U.S.
  • The agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, Upcoming York. A genetic condition gave it the color, and it went to Cornell.

Sources indicate that biologists with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service were running a routine survey in Oswego Harbor, New York, on Lake Ontario, in October when they pulled up a fish they did not expect. It was a burbot, and it was bright yellow-orange.

The agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch. The fish has xanthochromism, a rare condition that gives it a saturated yellow-orange color.

The agency stated the fish would make even the brightest fall foliage look pale in comparison.

It is also the first burbot ever documented during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few anglers have reported catching them there.

Xanthochromism is caused by a genetic mutation that suppresses normal pigmentation and produces the yellow-orange appearance.

It is considerably less common in wild fish than albinism or melanism, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service. Unusual colors like this have surprised scientists before, as with a bright orange shark.

The place was a surprise too. Burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species usually lives in deeper, cooler water than what is found inside the harbor.

The crew was not looking for burbot. It came from the Lower Great Lakes Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office, and it was carrying out an Aquatic Invasive Species survey.

The program watches harbors, rivers and bays of the Great Lakes for invasive species on a watchlist.

Because invaders are often rare when they first arrive, the crews use several methods at once, including electrofishing, fyke nets, gill nets and environmental DNA, or eDNA.

Invaders are an old problem in these waters: the Great Lakes have been under invasion from one species for 70 years.

Recent findings suggest that most fish caught in these surveys are native species. Catching a rare native fish suggests the program may also detect newly arriving invaders when their numbers are still very low.

The agency summed it up as an effective survey strategy, along with a bit of luck.

The burbot is a native fish of the Great Lakes. It tends to live on the lake bottom, and it is the only cod-like fish species in freshwater, according to a Latest York Sea Grant fact sheet. The same fact sheet calls it a formidable predator.

In the Great Lakes, sea lamprey predation has been a common factor affecting burbot numbers.

A 2006 study led by U.S. Geological Survey scientists found that burbot abundance in eastern Lake Erie increased significantly between 1987 and 2003.

The researchers, writing in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society, attributed the apparent recovery to effective sea lamprey control.

The same study suggested that a relatively high density of alewives, a small plankton-eating fish, probably held burbot numbers down in Lakes Ontario and Michigan at the time.

When U.S. Geological Survey fisheries biologists who know the species processed the yellow burbot, they noticed it was emaciated and looked to be in poor health.

Sources indicate that because of its condition, and because the reasons the species remains so scarce in the lake are still unexplained, the fish was sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis. The agency has not reported the results.

The agency says the catch could turn out to be lucky for the species too.

The rare fish may offer valuable insight into the health of burbot populations across the basin, and that could help guide how they are managed.

The information was obtained from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, a New York Sea Grant fact sheet and a U.S. Geological Survey study.

#77421. Independents decide the election, again!

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1171 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

Independents decide the election, again!

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E.
  • Recent findings suggest that once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep.
  • “We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Sources indicate that clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

Industry observers note that according to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top issue concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent mentioned it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent said his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic complications and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

According to recent reports, neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls revealed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

It has been revealed that independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

Recent findings suggest that at a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent mentioned the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

In a recent development, democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy complications, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

#77420. American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3442 w)

American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3442 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes.
  • It has been revealed that “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes. Lindsey, who until early 2025 managed the federal government’s climate.gov website, had just begun to think her job might be safe during the second Trump administration.

It has been revealed that “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years. “Every time you would hear the rumor and then it wouldn’t happen, you would think … maybe this is all just talk.”.

But at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer “fit the Agency’s current needs.” In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.

The Lindsey sisters decided to fight back. Along with another terminated NOAA employee, they split a $65,000 grant from the nonprofit Surge Climate Talent and debuted a crowdfunding campaign to rebuild and revision climate.gov. The site, now called climate.us, notched one million views in its first month.

But as proud as they are of their work, the project is a patch, not a fix. Rebecca Lindsey predicts it would take at least seven employees and $1.8 million annually to resume 80 percent of the old site’s work. “Climate.gov was more than just a website; it was a climate literacy program,” she says. To rescue the full mission, they still have a long way to go.

It has been revealed that courtesy of M. Lindsey and R. Lindsey.

It has been revealed that the Lindsey sisters are far from the only tale of makeshift resilience. Over the last year, untold numbers of U.S. scientists and their supporters have rebuilt data dashboards, formed recommendation groups for childhood vaccines and screenings, and doled out research funds for hundreds of stranded early-career scientists. They’ve reconstituted committees to advise space missions, rehomed key reports on climate and Arctic science, and even turned to social media to spread public health alerts in the wake of a massive realignment of the federal science enterprise.

“I don’t think anyone could have foreseen the amount of destruction and deliberate breaking down of norms and infrastructure” over the last two years, says Christina Madison, a clinical pharmacist and public health communicator known on social media as The Public Health Pharmacist.

Sources indicate that since January 2025, the second Trump administration has frozen or rescinded billions of dollars in research funding on topics from climate change to vaccine hesitancy and is trying to redirect it — often without congressional approval — to administration priorities such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. During deliberations for the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, the White House proposed slashing future science funding by one-third.

Industry observers note that “When this was first starting, it really, truly felt like an alternate universe,” notes Sean O’Leary, a pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “The science was always what drove the decision making, and now we’re at a place where it’s not.”.

In 2025 alone, the federal government shed some 20 percentof its science workforce. And in May 2026, the Office of Management and Budget proposed a sweeping set of rules to expand the authority of federal political appointees in selecting science grants.

Approximate proportion of the scientific workforce who left federal service in 2025.

Yet some researchers see the destruction as an opportunity to rebuild their corners of U.S. science — or even reimagine it, indicates Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “If there’s any good that can come out of what has been a horrible situation, it’s that it’s given us time and provided a pause to think through clearly: Is this the way we want to continue?”.

Recent findings suggest that university of Ottawa ecologist Julien Martin spent a decade building a respected lab that probed how social behaviors affect the evolution of bushy-tailed, cat-sized rodents called marmots. So when the National Science Foundation began its sweeping grant cuts, Martin found himself doing something unexpected: uploading cute marmot videos to OnlyFans, an online video subscription platform better known for hosting pornography.

The effort, called OnlyMarms, netted $6,000 — a mere drop in the funding bucket. But the project went viral, leading outside supporters to launch a cryptocurrency token that earned the lab an additional $150,000. And direct donations, including an anonymous $300,000 gift, gave the lab enough to fund one Ph.D. student’s entire degree.

According to recent reports, “When you see that so much money could be obtained by doing essentially nothing about science, it’s quite shocking,” Martin states. He welcomes the support, but having to spend so much time on non-research tasks has also felt demeaning. “Sometimes, you have to question: Is the science funding broken? Are we just competing for pennies?”.

Industry observers note that in 2025, the National Institutes of Health and the NSF canceled or suspended more than 7,800 existing grants, totaling billions of dollars. (Some 5,200 grants were later reinstated.) Each agency issued roughly a quarter fewer grants in 2025 than their previous 10-year averages.

Universities and research centers were hit hard. “It was really dire,” states Emily Young, who leads medical research grantmaking at the San Diego-based Prebys Foundation. In phone calls with researchers, many told her they had halted ongoing experiments, such as developing measles vaccines for people with autoimmune disorders.

Sources indicate that but the thing that really stood out, Young claims, was how the sudden drop in funding was affecting postdocs and early-career researchers. “Young people were going from feeling like they had an avenue for a really promising career … to feeling like they were in a worthless career.”.

So, in May 2025, the foundation awarded $7 million total in emergency grants to seven local institutions, including San Diego State University, the University of California, San Diego and Scripps Research. The grants targeted more than 80 research programs involving early- and mid-career scientists that were facing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost federal funding.

Larger science philanthropies also stepped into the breach. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $55 million total to 30 universities to support 400 postdoctoral researchers. The Alfred P. Sloan and Spencer foundations, among others, partnered to provide 83 quick-turnaround grants of around $25,000 each to researchers whose NSF education grants had been canceled.

Some wealthy universities also offered bridge funding to their researchers; Johns Hopkins University gave awards up to $250,000 to individuals with unexpected funding gaps, and the Yale School of Medicine arranged to fund up to 90 percent of terminated or frozen NIH grants.

After the first bout of funding chaos, science philanthropy Schmidt Sciences announced a more ambitious approach: to develop the science themselves. In January 2026, they revealed prepares to construct three ground-based observatories and a space telescope larger than NASA’s Hubble by the end of the decade. The space telescope alone will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and provide open-access data to scientists worldwide, with a special focus on exoplanets and transient events like supernovas.

In November 2026, the philanthropy opened its first round of funding for early-career scientists using the observatory system; individual awards will total up to $2.5 million each.

“Originally, the hope was we would play a more classic philanthropic role,” says Arpita Roy, an astronomer who directs the Astrophysics & Space Center at Schmidt Sciences. But given the federal funding landscape, she says, “it became pretty clear to us, if we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

While private funding can be a lifeline, Young claims, it’s still a temporary measure at best. “We are not going to fill the vacuum of federal funding,” she says. “There is simply not enough philanthropic resource out there to do that.”.

According to recent reports, in 1995, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made a consequential decision: Rather than publish independent recommendations for childhood vaccines, as they had since the 1960s, they would issue one set jointly. Over the next 30 years, a group called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices advised the CDC, with academy input, to expand its recommendations to include chickenpox, hepatitis A and pneumococcal infections. Cases of the three dropped by more than 90 percent, saving thousands of lives.

But in June 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an outspoken vaccine critic, fired all 17 members of ACIP and replaced many with vaccine skeptics. Kennedy also dismissed the academy representatives that informed the group.

In a recent development, “Essentially, we had no voice anymore,” recalls O’Leary, the pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. He also serves as the AAP’s immunization schedule editor. “So we made a decision to not participate until we could say, ‘OK, this is a body that can be trusted.’ ”.

It has been revealed that in July 2025, the academy and other public health groups sued over the ACIP firings. The committee was unable to meet due to the lawsuit, and over the next six months, the CDC removed recommendations from its childhood vaccination schedule including hepatitis A and B, COVID-19 and meningococcal disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics issued its own schedule including those vaccines in January 2026.

Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images Plus.

The loss of trustworthy federal recommendations leaves “an impossible gap to fill,” O’Leary says. But when it came to stepping in, “from my perspective, there was not an alternative.” The academy has since collaborated with the Vaccine Integrity Project, a newly introduced group led by Osterholm, to conduct the scientific reviews that inform vaccine recommendations.

According to recent reports, vaccines weren’t the only childhood health matter to get a shakeup. In April 2025, HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children, which formulates newborn screening recommendations for genetic disorders, many of which can be deadly or disabling. Currently, some 98 percent of U.S.-born infants are screened at birth.

In a recent development, when the genetics community raised concerns, Cynthia Powell, a retired pediatric geneticist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine in Chapel Hill, gathered around 15 representatives of professional medical societies to create the Newborn Screening Collaborative. With support from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, the group began meeting in early 2026.

While the collaborative cannot give direct recommendations to HHS, it hopes to conduct evidence reviews for states and the small, parent-led advocacy groups that form around rare diseases, Powell indicates. It looks to focus on conditions that already have treatments under development, like a rare metabolic disorder known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Approximate number of NIH and NSF grants canceled or suspended in 2025. Some 5,200 have since been reinstated.

“This Newborn Screening Collaborative is another effort not to leave a complete void,” says Jewel Mullen, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin who was lead editor on a May 2025 newborn screening report for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.

Industry observers note that other researchers are filling gaps in awareness about public health threats. A philanthropy-backed group called the Evidence Collective posted about the diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak before the CDC’s Health Alert Network did. The collective, made up of more than 30 medical communicators, has more than 10 million followers across social media and notched 11 billion impressions in 2025.

Industry observers note that “I don’t think that we will ever be able to fully replace the infrastructure that was there through the federal government,” says Madison, a founding member of the collective. But “there is a concerted effort now to look at: How do we take the momentum that we have with these organizations, and then make it sustainable?”.

Industry observers note that although stopgap measures are succeeding so far, scientists see them as Band-Aids at best. “We’re going to do it for as long as we’re needed,” Osterholm says. But “I look forward to the day when we’re not going to be needed anymore.”.

Sources indicate that in April 2025, nearly 400 scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, a recurring, congressionally mandated report, received an email that it was being reevaluated and they were being released from their work. One of them — Rutgers University climate scientist Bob Kopp — wasn’t surprised. “I don’t think you have to speculate very far” to know why, Kopp notes. He cites a directive in the White House’s 2027 budget request to “stop wasting biological and environmental research resources on climate change.”.

However, “there was an immediate and deep sentiment by the science community to continue the work,” indicates environmental engineer Costa Samaras of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who had also been involved with the climate report. He and colleagues asked the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society to help organize the U.S. Climate Collection, a newly introduced set of papers from scientists about climate research, risks and solutions that will keep the public informed until federal assessments resume.

While the work is promising, “a volunteer effort of 170 scientists cannot substitute for a $30 million effort of 600 people,” Kopp states.

The American Geophysical Union similarly stepped in with crucial financing for the Arctic Report Card, an annual report from NOAA that has provided information about the changing Arctic since 2006. Its editors were blindsided when they found out during a routine meeting in August 2026 that NOAA was withdrawing its support.

AGU’s in-kind offer to support the project just one month later was “tremendous,” says Twila Moon, a glaciologist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, Colo., who edits the report card. “But [it] is not a kind of model that is sustainable into the future.”.

In a recent development, AGU President Brandon Jones agrees. Nevertheless, at the time, the organization “had this sense of what was moral, what was right, what was ethical,” Jones says. And given AGU’s resources, “it seemed like it was our turn to show up and step up and act like the union that we’ve always been.”.

The Planetary Society, a nonprofit space advocacy organization based in Pasadena, Calif., took the lead on several committees that NASA dropped. In January, the agency cited executive orders as it withdrew financial and logistical support from eight groups of space scientists and experts that advised NASA’s planning teams on exploring asteroids, comets and planets.

“It was pretty well-managed and organized [before], and then really fell apart because of the intrusion of the executive orders,” states Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society. The organization now hosts the advisory groups’ websites, documents and meetings. “We’ve basically been having to reinvent this whole system.”.

Chris Gunn, Courtesy of Schmidt Sciences.

Recent findings suggest that climate.us isn’t the only site saving federal data. In November 2024, many environmental organizations “started preparing for the worst,” claims Brittany Janis, executive director of the Open Environmental Data Project. Her group and nine others banded together to create the Public Environmental Data Partners, a network of 400 volunteers that archive environmental data and tools they suspected “would probably be on the chopping block.”.

It has been revealed that in February 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency deleted a tool called EJScreen, which maps places where people face high levels of risk from environmental burdens such as hazardous waste and ozone. Within 48 hours, the partnership had stood up EJScreen on a fresh website, using open-source files to reverse engineer and refine the data pipelines. It has since received 1,000 views a month, Janis claims.

In a recent development, nearly $2 million in philanthropic funding has helped the project pay staff, host data and hire engineers. It has restored the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Future Risk Index, which projects county-level economic losses from climate change; the White House Council on Environmental Quality’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool, which identifies communities overburdened by pollution; and the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data tool, which maps infrastructure at risk of natural disasters.

“We should not misunderstand the administration’s closing off of this data [to mean] that they don’t think data is important,” Janis states. “They recognize how important it is — and how valuable it is to causes that they disagree with.”.

According to recent reports, at the University of Chicago, the Data Mirror Project preserves datasets larger than one terabyte, including those from the U.S. Census Bureau and the National Park Service. The project has a guiding principle: LOCKSS, which stands for lots of copies keeps stuff safe, says colead Lisa Chinn, who is head of research data services at the university library. An agency doesn’t have to delete its data to create problems, she adds. Firing website staff can lead to wonky links, corrupted files and pages that degrade into Wingdings gibberish.

The thought of losing all that data can be stressful, Janis indicates, but “there’s a lot of parachutes that have gone out.”.

Sources indicate that even as researchers, volunteers and scientific organizations pick up the pieces of the federal science enterprise, some are already imagining upcoming ways of shaping it. “The world was not perfect in 2024,” states Rutgers’ Kopp. “Reconstruction is an opportunity to improve upon the way things are done.”.

Recent findings suggest that to Mullen, the epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin, transparency is key. Fresh bodies like the Vaccine Integrity Project and the Newborn Screening Collaborative should make their meetings and deliberations as open as possible, she indicates, especially when “people think that those with the loudest voices or the biggest wallets are going to be the ones that have the greatest influence behind the scenes.”.

In a recent development, powell, of the Newborn Screening Collaborative, is hoping for greater efficiency in the disease recommendation process. Previously, it could take as long as three years to bring a condition from an initial vote to a final recommendation; with the collaborative, she hopes it could take one to three months.

Sources indicate that janis, of the Open Environmental Data Project, hopes to develop more creative and flexible data tools for researchers based on their needs. And Madison from the Evidence Collective and Martin of OnlyMarms believe that the science infrastructure needs to diversify its funding sources to prevent future shocks.

“If we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

Sources indicate that however, Janis notes that there are inherent risks in having the private sector support public goods such as open information. And Kopp warns that “attempts to replace something that was well-functioning … are not going to necessarily end up with something that is better or even as good as what was there before.”.

At the end of the day, one of the key elements in establishing a latest science system is “faith that you will still exist in a year or 10 years or maybe even 20 years,” indicates Katharine Jacobs, an environmental scientist who directed a previous National Climate Assessment under President Obama. Without stable institutional funding, “we are all essentially wasting our time, bashing our heads against the wall, trying to create a system that we can’t support,” Jacobs says.

For the Lindsey sisters, being involved in public service — even outside the government aegis — has been empowering, especially during what they see as an otherwise dark period for science.

They have raised more than $600,000 from individual donations since August 2025. And in February, they received a one-time grant from the Doris Duke Foundation and others that will cover their salaries and benefits until February 2027.

Sources indicate that “If we can get the money, I can see us doing this indefinitely,” Rebecca Lindsey notes. She still hopes to retire one day, and she fights off worries that the government might come knocking about their unsanctioned work. But “we had a public that trusted us,” she says about jumping into the fray. “It was a risk worth taking.”.

Latest Update: A peanut by a lamp can make a city crow warier than a passing human

  • Industry observers note that in 2019 and 2020, a team led by biologist Dave J.
  • On some mornings the peanuts had manufacturer: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a paper takeout box or a faux-wood lamp base.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With a lamp base beside the peanuts, feeding odds fell to 0.53 for city crows and 0.76 for country crows in a Binghamton study of 20 crow families.

Industry observers note that in 2019 and 2020, a team led by biologist Dave J. Colucci put out peanuts in the shell for 20 families of American crows around Ithaca, Newly introduced York. Ten families lived in town, and ten in farm fields and natural areas of the nearby Town of Dryden.

On some mornings the peanuts had manufacturer: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a paper takeout box or a faux-wood lamp base. Country crows held back more around the box, and city crows around the corn.

Sources indicate that city crows were also less likely to eat next to the lamp, the study by Colucci and Anne Clark of Binghamton University found. Other urban-rural differences in the paper had only weak support.

It has been revealed that colucci earned a PhD at Binghamton in 2025. Clark is an associate professor emerita of biological sciences there, the Binghamton University release of November 16, 2026, states. The paper came out online in Behavioral Ecology on October 22.

Each family’s territory got a feeding spot. The bait was 2 cups of raw, unsalted peanuts in a circle about 3 feet (1 meter) wide. They picked spots with little human traffic and no sign of predators or competitors.

In town these were parking lots, dead-end streets and parks in Ithaca, Lansing and Cayuga Heights. Out in Dryden the sites were on private or public land.

Each family got three days with peanuts only and four days with an object, 140 trials in total, each starting between 6 and 8 a.m.

It has been revealed that A hidden camcorder sat at least 10 feet (3 meters) from the bait. The observer stayed 164 feet (50 meters) or more away.

The team ranked the objects by how often a crow in each place would have seen them. Rocks are everywhere and corn grows in Dryden, while takeout boxes are more common in town.

“What we wanted to show was that aversion would decrease with the amount of experience that we expected our crow to have had with these objects,” Colucci noted in the release.

According to recent reports, to test the trash part, the team surveyed a 1-mile (1.61-kilometer) road route in each area weekly for three weeks. They counted 341 human-made objects, 169 in town and 172 in the country. Rural ones stayed put longer, 2.81 weeks on average against 2.27.

The box cut feeding more for rural crows and the corn cut it more for urban crows. But the paper says the evidence for that switch was limited.

It has been revealed that crows that live near an Arby’s or a McDonald’s learn to recognize that chain’s boxes, Clark remarked in the release. The box in the test was a plain one with no brand.

Recent findings suggest that the lamp base was supposed to be upcoming to every crow, in town or out. The authors chose it because it has none of the usual signs of a human-made thing, like bright colors, shine or sharp corners.

In a recent development, with peanuts alone, nearly every visit ended in feeding, a probability of 0.99 in town and 0.97 in Dryden. Put the lamp down and it fell to 0.53 for urban crows and 0.76 for rural crows, according to the paper’s Bayesian model.

How fast the birds came in was another matter. Timing for the boldest crow in each family was about the same in both places with the lamp out. That held for reaching 10 feet (3 meters) of the bait and for taking a first peanut.

It has been revealed that overall, the urban families did reach the bait sooner, at 4.23 times the rural rate. The authors attribute this to the rural crows partly reacting to the person on watch, since country crows are warier of people.

Earlier work had mostly found that city birds are bolder with new things, which is why the release calls this somewhat surprising. Clark noted urban crows “are social animals” that watch one another. “In an area that has a lot of new opportunities, there are also new threats,” she said.

The second test was about people. An experimenter walked toward single crows and noted how close the walker got before each one flew, a figure biologists call flight initiation distance.

In a recent development, one person did all 145 trials, in upstate New York and in Quebec, in 2019, 2022 and 2023. The pace was a steady 2.7 miles per hour (1.2 meters per second). On some walks the experimenter looked at the crow, and on others tilted the whole face down.

In a recent development, on average the crows took off when the walker was about 149 feet (45.3 meters) away. The walker got closer than 33 feet (10 meters) only 8 times. Where the walker looked mattered only in more crowded places.

The model looked at areas with about 13,000 people per square mile (5,000 per square kilometer). There, it put the distance for a downward look near zero, about 82 feet (25 meters) shorter than for a stare. Rural crows left at about the same distance either way.

Sources indicate that the authors warn that those predictions are uncertain. Human population within about half a mile (800 meters) of each trial predicted flight distance best.

Crow hunting is allowed in rural Fresh York in a set season but prohibited within city limits, the paper notes. The release says crows, seen as a nuisance, are more likely to be shot in rural areas.

Clark called the rural behavior “a blunt, anti-predator strategy” in the release. “Whereas in urban areas, if you were fleeing at every human, you’d never spend any time on the ground,” she stated.

The authors compare the gaze result with earlier work on Seattle crows, where flight distance was on average about 10.5 feet (3.2 meters) shorter for an indirect gaze.

Recent findings suggest that separate University of Washington mask experiments found that wild crows learned the faces of dangerous people and passed the details to other crows. They remembered a threatening person for up to 17 years.

Separate lab work in Germany found carrion crows that made decisions about twice as fast as humans in a visual task.

It has been revealed that the town sites were really suburban, the authors say, not downtown. The litter count covered roadsides at one site per area, and the timing data on approaches came from 2020 only.

One person ran every flight trial, and the approach timings may partly reflect wariness of the experimenter. Census numbers may also miss parks and shopping areas, where few people live but many walk through.

The lamp may not have been fully new to city crows either. It is perfectly symmetrical around its vertical axis, a shape rare in nature and common in things people make. So the town-country gap could be underestimated, the paper states.

In Ithaca and Dryden, the 20 crow families got the same peanuts. What sat next to them, and who was walking by, changed what they did.

The full study was published in the journal Behavioral Ecology.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, unlike window air conditioners, portable air conditioners roll easily from room to room and take only minutes to set up—no brackets, no tools, no sweating through a complicated installation before you can start sweating less. Most just require a nearby window and wall outlet to get cold air flowing. Yes, they tend to cost a bit more than window units, but the tradeoff is real: you can’t beat the convenience their portability adds, which is why many people choose them over other models. Plus your view isn’t blocked by a giant metal box.

According to recent reports, portable air conditioners have an internal fan that moves hot, humid air over a refrigerant-gas-filled coil to cool and expel it into a room to lower the temperature. The moisture it strips from the air collects in an internal reservoir that you’ll periodically need to drain. Higher-end units either pump it out automatically or evaporate it entirely so you never have to think about it. Because the whole unit rolls on casters, you can take the cold air with you instead of running more energy intensive central a/c or buying multiple window units.

To find the best models to recommend, we tested air conditioners from trusted brands like LG, GE, Black + Decker, Midea, Hisense, and more. These are the units that stood out and are worth the investment.

Recent findings suggest that we placed each unit in its own room and directed its discharge hose to the outside, then set the appliance’s temperature to 68 degrees and its fan speed to maximum. We directed the cold air each unit discharged at a target 8 feet away, then used an infrared thermometer to measure the temperature at four different locations on the target. We also checked the appliance’s outlet to see if it maintained a consistent temperature. To test the wheels’ durability and noise, we rolled each unit on a hard surface to maximize squeaks and rattles.

We also sent several air conditioners to our staff’s homes and apartments for further testing, where our editors used them over the course of weeks within the living spaces. We tested how easy they were to use, how they operated over time, and how easy they were to integrate into daily life.

From there, we narrowed the field by prioritizing units with strong efficiency ratings, straightforward setup, and drainage designs that won’t require constant attention.

The unit has three modes: cooling, fan, and dry. Cooling and fan are pretty straightforward while dry actually turns the unit into a dehumidifier. So, when you don’t actively need it, feel free to have it run in moist spaces like your laundry room or garage.

The louvers on the a/c unit can be set to move up and down on their own. This actually made a pretty notable difference in full-room air circulation and helped get rid of hot air that sat near the ceiling.

The portable air conditioner has a dual-hose design (intake and exhaust) for reducing the amount of condensate that the a/c collects, since it’s supposed to be removed in the exhaust air stream.

It has been revealed that while most units are either quiet or powerful, the GE Profile Portable A/C offers a bit of both worlds. This was definitely true during testing.

On its average setting, the a/c noticeably cooled down a mid-sized room in less than ten minutes. Holding up my hand to the vents, I felt a cold blast of air much stronger than other options I tried out. Going even further, the Profile has a turbo mode that turns the fans up to an even higher level.

According to recent reports, the effectiveness of the cooling has do to with more than just airflow, too. This portable a/c unit also comes with auto louvers that more evenly distribute cold air by shifting the vents up and down. I particularly like this feature for apartments like mine which are a few floors up and end up with a lot of accumulated hot air near the ceiling. The auto louvers help bring down the temperature of the entire room down as opposed to just blasting cold air in one direction.

While all these features impressed me, the unit’s best quality is that it doesn’t stand out at all. This a/c is incredibly quiet. While I barely noticed the sound at normal levels, when I set the unit to quiet mode, the noise levels drop to a whisper. According to GE, quiet mode is measured at just 42 decibels, which is lower than all other options we recommend.

Recent findings suggest that if the other units on this list take up more real estate than you have or want to give, the Dreo AC319S is the one you won’t have to make room for. Be warned, though, the tradeoff for that smaller footprint is smaller cooling coverage. This one is best for bedrooms, home offices, and other spaces up to 300 square feet.

But what it gives up in cooling-size capabilities, it makes up for in smart features and low maintenance. That kind of hands-off convenience is why this one made our list.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re fortunate to have a large living room, an open-strategy studio, or a finished basement, you know the luxury of size comes with a cost—cooling oversized areas can be tough. To beat the heat in big rooms, the Whynter ARC-1230WN is the unit we’d point you toward.

Industry observers note that with 14,000 BTUs, it covers up to 600 square feet—more than any other unit on this list. In independent testing, it dropped room temperature by about 12 degrees in a single hour, a result no other unit came close to matching.

A substantial part of that performance comes from Whynter's hose-in-hose dual-hose design. Unlike a standard dual-hose setup, the intake and exhaust lines run concentrically inside a single tube, preventing heat leakage between the airstreams and improving overall efficiency. The inverter compressor, which ramps up and down rather than cycling on and off, keeps noise down once the room reaches your set temperature and reduces energy use.

Industry observers note that according to Whynter, the inverter technology delivers 20 percent more cooling capacity and over 40 percent energy savings compared to non-inverter models. The dual-hose design pulls in fresh air and expels exhaust air through a single concentric hose, keeping a neutral pressure balance in rooms. According to recent reports, the unit provides multiple fan speeds, dedicated dehumidification, a timer setting, and a sleep setting. Note that there is no heater setting on this appliance. It’s meant to cool and dehumidify exclusively.

Sources indicate that reviews Editor Amber Joglar tested out the four-in-one version of this model which also functions as a heater. After just 10 minutes of use in her room, Joglar felt, “a noticeable shift in the air temperature.”.

The quick cooldown times stood out across both models, though Joglar also pointed out that this led to the exhaust pipes heating up rapidly as well. This isn’t necessarily a problem, but if you plan on using the unit for several hours a day, consider covering the tubes in insulation.

In addition to the cold air, Joglar liked the remote and LED control panel, saying, “I normally just change settings on the air conditioner itself because it’s right next to my bed, so backlit controls are helpful.”.

Similarly, the remote control is great for when she’s already in bed or wants to pre-cool the room before she’s ready to go to sleep.

Read Our Full Black+Decker Portable Air Conditioner Review.

Coverage area is one of the most vital factors in choosing an air conditioner. Manufacturers rate units in square footage, but that number assumes an average ceiling height (roughly eight feet) and room insulation. If the room is especially hot in the summer (for example, it’s a finished attic or it has large, south-facing windows) we recommend bumping up to the next size rather than buying a unit that will run constantly and struggle to keep up.

According to recent reports, an air conditioner’s cooling capacity is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTU, per hour. To gauge coverage, figure roughly 20 BTU per square foot of space. Most portable a/c units range from 5,000 to 20,000 BTUs, which puts their effective range roughly between 350 and 700 square feet. So when in doubt, size up—an oversized unit cycles off when it hits your target temperature, while an undersized one never stops trying.

Single-hose units essentially recirculate the room’s air to cool it and have one line that runs outdoors to expel exhaust. The catch is that expelling air creates a slight negative pressure in the room, which pulls in warm air from other parts of the house and from outside through gaps around doors and windows. It works, but it’s working against itself.

Dual-hose units solve this by pulling outside air in through one hose for cooling and pushing hot exhaust out through a second hose. The result is a more self-contained system that’s noticeably more efficient, especially in larger spaces. The tradeoff is price.

Industry observers note that because dual-hose models are more complex, they tend to be more expensive. If you only have a small space to cool, a portable a/c with a single hose may suit your needs just fine. For anything larger, the dual-hose design is worth seriously considering.

Recent findings suggest that hose length determines how far away from a window you can maneuver your portable air conditioner. If you set it up in a large room, or one where the nearest window is far from where most people gather, hose length becomes more key.

It also plays a key role in room setup. If the hose isn’t long enough to set the air conditioner in front of large furniture pieces, you may have to rearrange the room for the most effective cooling. Most hoses range anywhere from 50 to 90 inches fully extended. This should give you enough space to make adjustments and pull the air conditioner closer to the center of the room if needed.

Most portable air conditioners hover between 50 and 60 decibels while they’re running—that’s roughly the noise level of a normal conversation. In most cases, that’s fine during the day, but if you’re planning to run the unit in a bedroom overnight, those numbers start to matter.

Sources indicate that units that dip below 50 decibels in their quietest modes are on par with most ceiling fans and are easier to sleep through; a few on this list get impressively close to whisper-quiet. Pay attention to the decibel rating at the unit’s lowest fan setting, not just its average operating level.

Recent findings suggest that much like larger ductless mini-split air conditioners, some portable air conditioners include a heat pump. “If you’re shopping for an a/c unit because you have a space not at the moment cooled or heated, one of these models may warrant consideration,” says gear editor Bradley Ford. “Similarly, you may have a room that your HVAC system doesn’t reach effectively. Rooms like this are typically either too cold or hot, depending on the season. If this is the case, a unit with heating capabilities may be able to fill your HVAC gap.”.

Industry observers note that every portable a/c pulls moisture out of the air, similar to home dehumidifiers. The question is what happens to it next. Budget units collect it in an internal pan that you’ll need to manually drain, sometimes daily in humid conditions.

Industry observers note that other units use self-evaporating technology to push moisture out through the exhaust hose with no bucket to remember. A few high-end models go even further, offering a continuous drainage port where you can attach a hose and never think about water again. If low-maintenance matters to you, the drainage method is a factor to consider.

There isn’t a clear superior option between window units and portable options. Choosing between the two largely depends on your home, windows, and personal needs. That said, window air conditioning units are generally faster at bringing temperatures down and run more efficiently than their portable counterparts.

Portable air conditioners have certainly closed the gap over time in terms of cooling ability, but still lag behind if that’s your number one priority.

Portable units stand out because of their convenience and ease of setup. If you don’t have compatible windows, get a portable unit. If you need quick cooling in a spot that generally doesn’t need air conditioning, get a portable unit. If you want just one machine for your entire apartment, get a portable unit.

Portable air conditioners are compatible with a lot more window openings than window units, so you can use them regardless of your apartment or home fixtures.

According to recent reports, new portable a/c units are relatively energy efficient across the board. That said, it’s certainly a sliding scale. There are several ways in which energy efficiency is calculated for air conditioners, but the shorthand is if your a/c unit is Energy Star-certified, it’s worth getting.

It has been revealed that for items that don’t have Energy Star certification, pay attention to the CEER, EER, and SEER numbers. In short, look for an air conditioner with a CEER above 10, with anything above 12 qualifying for Energy Star certification. Similarly, look out for a SEER above 14 in the north and 15 in the south as well as an EER above 10. These are general numbers, but serve as a basic guide when choosing between different options.

In a recent development, one of the biggest challenges to solve with portable air conditioners is cooling efficiency. While most units generate a ton of cold air, leakage from the hose or exhaust port can work against that. There are two key things you can do: insulate the opening in the window and insulate the hose itself.

In a recent development, many portable units provide foam pieces that fit in and around the window insert to minimize the amount of hot air that leaks in from outside. The hose itself won’t come with foam insulation pieces, but you can perform a similar trick by buying one online or by making one yourself. Some people use blankets while others have used everything from reflective sun shades to Amazon plastic packaging. The goal is to prevent heat from the tube from radiating into your living space.

Fossil teeth challenge a long-held idea about where early humans could live

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in rainforests and survived in the region longer than scientists thought.
  • Dense tropical rainforest was long regarded as a habitat that only our own species, Homo sapiens, had mastered.
  • It has been revealed that homo erectus, an extinct human relative, spread from Africa across Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in rainforests and survived in the region longer than scientists thought.

Dense tropical rainforest was long regarded as a habitat that only our own species, Homo sapiens, had mastered.

It has been revealed that homo erectus, an extinct human relative, spread from Africa across Asia. It was thought to need grassland and open woodland.

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in a rainforest landscape.

They are also far younger than any other firmly dated fossil of the species on the Chinese mainland.

The study was led by Kira Westaway at Macquarie University in Sydney and Renaud Joannes-Boyau at Southern Cross University. Colleagues in China and Europe also took part.

Only a handful of teeth were found, and their dates span a broad window. By the team’s estimate, the species was present sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.

The two caves are known as Baxian and Naxian. Both are found in Guangxi, among steep limestone hills, roughly 9 miles (15 kilometers) from each other.

At the back of each cave sits a small chamber where fossils have been cemented into rock. More than 18,000 mammal fossils have been recovered from these chambers.

Porcupines may have brought many of the fossils into the caves.

Nine of those fossils were teeth from ancient humans.

Researchers assigned eight of the nine teeth to Homo erectus based on their shape, with ancient enamel proteins supporting the identification of four.

It has been revealed that researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing were part of the team. The institute also provided access to the excavated fossils.

Westaway’s team used five independent methods to date the teeth and the cave deposits around them.

Two of them work out when grains of sediment were last exposed to sunlight. The rest rely on uranium, which decays slowly in the teeth and in a mineral crust capping the fossils.

In total, 45 ages were obtained. Forty-three of them were fed into a statistical model.

The model gave a 95% probability that Homo erectus was there sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.

It has been revealed that that span is a measure of how uncertain the dates are. It doesn’t mean the species stayed there for all 140,000 years.

The latest teeth date to between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, making them younger than the previous firmly dated finds in China, which were about 400,000 years old.

“This is a fascinating discovery because it confirms the presence of Homo erectus in a location we were not expecting and at a time we hadn’t considered,” Westaway said.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere, the species hung on even longer. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java show it there until roughly 117,000 to 108,000 years ago.

What an animal eats is written into its tooth enamel as chemistry. Carbon from trees and shrubs looks different there from carbon taken in from tropical grasses.

So by testing a tooth, scientists can tell whether its owner fed in forest or in open country.

No signature of tropical grasses was found in the teeth that were tested.

According to recent reports, many values were low enough to indicate a dense, closed canopy. A similar pattern has been recorded in forests of the western Amazon.

It has been revealed that the mix of species fits this picture. Orangutans, elephants, rhinoceroses and tapirs were found among the fossils. Most of the animals were forest dwellers.

Recent findings suggest that other chemical tests pointed to a humid climate. Conditions were wetter and cooler than in the region today.

Industry observers note that three Homo erectus teeth from Naxian were then tested in the same way. Their carbon values fell in the same forest range.

Those readings fell right where dense canopy gives way to more open forest.

Nicolas Bourgon, affiliated with the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany, also took part in the research.

“In this case, the animal teeth and the Homo erectus teeth are telling the same story,” said Bourgon.

In a recent development, strontium is locked into enamel as well. It’s picked up from local rock by water and plants, and animals take it in when they eat and drink. Each type of rock has its own strontium signature.

Industry observers note that teeth form in childhood, between the ages of 2 and 6. Their strontium therefore records where a child’s food and water came from.

In a recent development, strontium was measured in four Homo erectus teeth. One came from Baxian and three came from Naxian. Each tooth carried signatures from more than one kind of rock.

So each child either moved between regions, or else ate food that had been gathered from several places.

A few of those signatures were consistent with the limestone near the caves.

The most extreme ones best matched rock about 155 miles (250 kilometers) to the south. That area lies toward the Red River valley in northern Vietnam.

“This suggests these humans were far more mobile than previously recognized, moving across surprisingly large distances through a complex rainforest landscape,” Joannes-Boyau said.

Still, the strontium evidence was called limited by the authors, and their reading of it tentative.

Rainforest has played a part in the debate over how Homo erectus died out.

On Java, the last known members of the species lived in open woodland. Rainforest was expanding around them at the time.

It has been revealed that it has been proposed that the spreading forest contributed to the extinction there. In this view, the species could not adapt to it.

The teeth from Guangxi complicate that idea. Homo erectus was “not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments,” the authors wrote.

Scientists use the word hominin for humans and our extinct close relatives.

“This is the first clear, direct evidence we have for another hominin living within these habitats,” mentioned Patrick Roberts, also of the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

The date range also overlaps with fossils of Denisovans, another extinct human group. Their remains have been found in Laos, on the Tibetan Plateau, in northeastern China and off Taiwan.

The authors wrote that several kinds of humans may have lived across the region during the same period.

The case for rainforest life rests on very few human teeth. Carbon values were obtained from only three of them, and all three came from one cave.

It has been revealed that the teeth show that Homo erectus could survive among rainforest animals. They cannot show that the species did well there.

The authors also wrote that rainforest may not have been its ideal habitat.

Recent findings suggest that it remains unclear whether this ability was limited to late survivors in southern China. It may also have been shared by the species more widely.

To settle that question, the same enamel tests will be needed on fossils from other sites of a similar age.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to matter subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

According to recent reports, the letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter claims.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

It has been revealed that “The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”.

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself stated that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and Upcoming York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the latest Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

In a recent development, garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin noted.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.
